title: 3-Read Friday #122
author: Barton, Craig
summary: In this issue of his weekly roundup, Craig Barton curates and comments on three education blog posts covering PISA 2025, note-taking pedagogy, and the design of anti-cheating interventions in schools. On Greg Ashman's PISA analysis, Barton flags the uncomfortable finding for progressive-education advocates that England has held steady while Scotland, Wales, and the OECD average continue to decline, undercutting both Finland-as-model and Japan's-active-learning narratives. On Dylan Kane's piece against reliance on student notes, Barton connects it to his own prior writing ('The Myth of Copying Down') and a podcast conversation with Jo Morgan, summarizing Kane's argument that writing is valuable for learning but that requiring students to later reference their own notes carries a real opportunity cost and is not the transferable skill teachers often assume. On Adam Grant's piece about school cheating, Barton adds his own sharp working hypothesis — that in the age of AI, any assessment conducted outside the classroom now has 'zero validity' because cheating is so easy — before summarizing Grant's argument that exam redesign and honesty pledges only treat symptoms, that a pledge in one experiment actually doubled cheating, and that the real fix lies in deliberately building students' moral identity, evidenced by an unrelated profession's ethics training.
points: Greg Ashman's PISA 2025 analysis, as summarized by Barton, shows England holding broadly steady while Scotland, Wales, and the OECD average continue to decline, undercutting narratives crediting Finland's model or Japan's active-learning reforms.
Barton states his own working hypothesis that in the age of AI, any assessment conducted outside the classroom now has 'zero validity' because it is too easy for students to cheat on it.

Dylan Kane's piece argues that while writing things down aids learning, requiring students to later reference their own notes carries a real opportunity cost and is not the reliably transferable skill teachers often assume.

Adam Grant's piece, per Barton's summary, found that asking students to sign an honesty pledge before an exam actually doubled the rate of cheating in one experiment, undercutting a common anti-cheating intervention.
Grant's proposed fix is building students' moral identity rather than redesigning exams or adding pledges, illustrated with evidence Barton describes as coming from 'an unlikely profession.'
